extracted.intended_audience: USPTO policymakers, patent practitioners, industry stakeholders, and legislators
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes public criticisms, sector-specific views, and recommended judicial, administrative, and legislative measures regarding patent subject matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101 (Mayo/Alice framework). Intended to guide policymakers and practitioners on how eligibility should be interpreted and applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conflating § 101 with §§ 102/103/112
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility analysis should not import considerations of novelty, nonobviousness, or written description; §§ 102, 103, and 112 are the appropriate statutory tools to address claims that are overly broad or preemptive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics argued that preemption analysis in Mayo/Alice 'has conflated eligibility with the more rigorous patentability requirements set forth in 35 U.S.C. §§ 102 and 103' and that the eligibility test 'has effectively evolved into a watered-down obviousness analysis.' Several commenters recommended using §§ 102, 103, and 112 to address overly broad claims rather than § 101.

rubrics_metrics.name: When eligibility is a close question, err on the side of eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: If a close question of patent eligibility arises, the USPTO should lean toward finding the claim eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some practitioners recommended that when a close question of patent eligibility arises the USPTO should 'err on the side of eligibility' to avoid denying rights where uncertainty exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constrict eligibility rulings narrowly (limit scope of judicial exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret Supreme Court jurisprudence narrowly to avoid expansive application of judicial exceptions (abstract ideas, laws of nature, natural phenomena) that unduly restrict subject matter eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple commenters urged the USPTO and courts to 'construe the Supreme Court’s ruling narrowly' to reduce inconsistency and overbroad ineligibility, preserving eligibility for meritorious inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess claims as a whole rather than 'stripping away' conventional limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility analysis should consider the claim in its entirety and not remove or ignore conventional elements as if performing an obviousness analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism: the Mayo/Alice framework 'fails to consider the claim as a whole, as during an obviousness analysis, but to instead “strip away” what are viewed as conventional limitations.' Commenters urged treating the claim holistically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use §§ 102/103/112 to address overbroad or vague claiming (preemption concerns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that threaten to preempt downstream innovation should be dealt with via novelty, nonobviousness, enablement, written description, or definiteness analyses rather than by expanding § 101 exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many members of the public argued that 'there are other more robust statutory grounds to address broad claims that “might preempt or prevent access to any underlying concept,” namely, lack of adequate written description, enablement, and definiteness.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve patent incentives—avoid interpretations that stifle innovation or shift to trade secrets
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility standards should not be so restrictive as to reduce incentives to innovate, cause businesses to rely on trade secrets, or disadvantage startups relative to incumbents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters warned that an overly broad application of judicial exceptions could 'eviscerate patent law,' diminish incentives to innovate, and push innovators to choose trade secret protection, reducing public disclosure and downstream benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider international norms and TRIPS compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: When revising or interpreting eligibility, ensure consistency with international obligations (e.g., TRIPS Article 27) and with patentability practices in other major jurisdictions to avoid disadvantaging U.S. innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several commenters raised concerns about inconsistency with international norms and argued amendments to § 101 should 'ensure TRIPS compliance' and consider harmonization to simplify multi-jurisdiction prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Life sciences: treat isolation or application of natural products as potentially eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: In the life sciences, isolating a natural product (or applying it in a new or different way) should, in some cases, be sufficient for subject matter eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Life sciences commentators argued that 'the act of isolating a natural product should be sufficient for patent subject matter eligibility, at least when isolation permits the product to be used or applied in a new or different way.' Studies were cited showing substantial impacts on drug/diagnostic claims if Myriad/Mayo are strictly applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide more and better examples in USPTO guidance (especially life sciences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Revise examination guidelines to include additional concrete examples of eligible subject matter and examples showing how ineligible claims might be rewritten to be eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal associations recommended amending § 101 examination guidelines to provide further guidance and more examples; commenters were disappointed that current examples do not show how to rewrite claims to be patent eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require examiners to provide detailed eligibility reasoning and rebut applicant arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should be required to set out detailed reasoning for § 101 rejections (analogous to prior art rejections) and to specifically address applicants’ arguments rather than dismissing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters suggested examiners be required to provide detailed reasoning on eligibility and to 'specifically rebut applicants' arguments' to create a fuller, clearer record and reduce perceived inconsistency and forum-shopping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid bright-line tests in diagnostics; appreciate diagnostic claim structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners and guidelines should not apply inflexible bright-line rules to diagnostic claims and should take into account how diagnostics are claimed and operate in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A diagnostics-industry commentator urged examiners to 'guard against application of bright line tests and to “appreciate how diagnostics work and how the claims typically sought in diagnostic medicine differ from decades-old claims held in court decisions to simply recite a law of nature.”'

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify eligibility of computer-implemented inventions; provide balanced guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO guidelines should clarify when computer software and computer-implemented claims are patent eligible, while also explaining limits (e.g., that mere recitation of a generic computer cannot transform an abstract idea).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some commenters recommended revising guidance to make clear that claims directed to computer software may be eligible; others warned the guidelines should not unfairly tilt toward eligibility. One non-profit recommended MPEP include Alice’s holding that 'mere recitation of a generic computer cannot transform a patent-ineligible abstract idea into a patent-eligible invention.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify and define 'technical solution' / 'technical problem' language
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO (and courts) should define what constitutes a 'technical solution to a technical problem' to provide examiners and practitioners with a predictable standard for software and related fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters noted the Federal Circuit's use of 'technical solution/technical problem' and urged the USPTO to clarify this terminology and explain how it should be applied in claims and the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: MPEP should explain Alice’s relationship to prior authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Amend the Manual of Patent Examining Procedure to explain how Alice overruled prior cases (or its limits), so examiners understand applicable precedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EFF recommended the MPEP include a clear explanation of how Alice overruled prior authority or at least reaffirm Alice’s holding on generic computers to guide examiners consistent with case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow judiciary to continue developing § 101 case law (common law evolution)
rubrics_metrics.description: One policy option is to defer to courts and allow Federal Circuit/district courts time to refine eligibility standards through case-by-case decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supporters of this approach cited historical churn after major precedent (e.g., KSR) and welcomed recent Federal Circuit decisions (Enfish, Amdocs, McRO, Rapid Litigation) as evidence courts can develop workable 'set of standards' over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pursue legislative reform to replace Mayo/Alice with a technological/useful arts test
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislative proposals include abrogating the two-part Mayo/Alice test in favor of a statutory technological or 'useful arts' requirement—focusing eligibility on technological contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many commenters (particularly life sciences) argued Congress should recalibrate § 101, with some proposals calling explicitly to 'replace Two-Part Test With Technological or Useful Arts Test.' Appendix IV of the report collects full legislative recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative measures to promote consistency and reduce forum-shopping
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt USPTO administrative changes—e.g., clearer guidelines, examiner training, explanatory examples, and requirements for reasoning—to achieve consistency across art units and reduce art-unit forum-shopping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters observed perceived inconsistency in examiner treatment of § 101 leading to 'forum-shopping' and proposed administrative steps to make examination more uniform and predictable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider economic and sectoral impacts (software and life sciences special concerns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy and claim-examination standards should account for industry-specific effects—particularly in life sciences (diagnostics/pharma) and software—on investment, commercialization, and U.S. competitiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public comments noted disproportionate impacts: life sciences claim narrowing threatens biopharma incentives and commercialization; software industry is split but some say Alice reduced abusive litigation and improved clarity; harmonization and predictable eligibility were urged to protect domestic industries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide guidance on rewriting ineligible claims to be eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance should include examples or instructions showing how applicants can amend or redraft claims that might be deemed ineligible so they recite patent-eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AIPLA and others criticized current examples for failing to show how to revise ineligible claims and recommended guidance that demonstrates concrete claim-drafting strategies to achieve eligibility.
